name: Sincalide
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in 1976 as a diagnostic agent and still marketed, with a second version approved in 2022. It is a test drug given once during an imaging study, not a treatment.
summary: A synthetic eight-amino-acid piece of the gut hormone CCK, given by IV during scans to make the gallbladder contract and test how well it empties.
keyTakeaway: Sincalide is a synthetic copy of the last eight amino acids of cholecystokinin, the gut hormone that makes the gallbladder squeeze. Sold as Kinevac since 1976, it is a diagnostic drug: given by IV during imaging, it makes the gallbladder contract so doctors can measure how much bile it empties, and it is also used to collect pancreatic juice and speed barium through the bowel. A 60-minute infusion gives the most consistent readings, and a gallbladder ejection fraction under 38% is considered abnormal. Nausea and abdominal discomfort are common.

blocks.text: Sincalide is a laboratory-made octapeptide, a chain of eight amino acids, matching the C-terminal end of cholecystokinin (CCK) [1]. CCK is a natural digestive hormone, and because sincalide is its final eight amino acids it is often called CCK-8 [1].

It is a diagnostic drug rather than a treatment. Given by vein during an imaging test, it makes the gallbladder contract and empty, so doctors can see whether the organ is working normally [1]. It is sold as Kinevac by Bracco, and MAIA Pharmaceuticals sells an equivalent version [2][3].

Kinevac was approved in the United States in 1976 as a new molecular entity [2]. MAIA filed its own version, which the FDA rates as therapeutically equivalent to Kinevac, and received approval in November 2022 [3].

items.text: Multicentre study sets the standard 60-minute infusion and normal ejection fraction values [4]
FDA approves MAIA's sincalide for injection [3]
Kinevac label adds stronger warnings on anaphylaxis and a sulfite allergy contraindication [1]

blocks.text: Sincalide acts like the body's own CCK. Injected into a vein, it makes the gallbladder contract and shrink, emptying bile in much the same way as the body's own CCK does [1]. After a single 0.02 mcg/kg injection, the strongest contraction came within 5 to 15 minutes, and a drop in gallbladder size of at least 40% is generally treated as a satisfactory squeeze [1].

It has other effects on the digestive tract. It stimulates the pancreas to secrete, increases movement of the intestine, tightens the pylorus (the valve at the stomach outlet), and slows stomach emptying [1]. Given together with secretin, another gut hormone, it boosts the volume of pancreatic fluid and its output of bicarbonate and enzymes, which lets doctors analyse a sample to judge how the pancreas is working [1].

Yes. Kinevac was approved on July 21, 1976 and remains a prescription product [2]. MAIA's sincalide for injection was approved on November 22, 2022 [3]. Both are 5 mcg vials of powder mixed and given by vein [1][3].

All approved uses are diagnostic and limited to adults; safety and effectiveness in children have not been established [1]. Sincalide is not approved to treat gallbladder disease, digestive symptoms, or appetite, and it is not taken at home.
The label lists three uses in adults [1]:

items: Making the gallbladder contract during imaging, or to collect a concentrated bile sample from the duodenum for analysis of cholesterol, bile salts, and crystals [1]
Stimulating pancreatic secretion together with secretin before taking a duodenal sample to test enzyme activity and look at cells [1]
Speeding a barium meal through the small bowel, which shortens X-ray and fluoroscopy time and the radiation that comes with it [1]

blocks.text: One use is cholescintigraphy, often called a HIDA scan, a nuclear medicine test that tracks a radioactive tracer through the liver and gallbladder. A 2010 study in 60 healthy volunteers at four centres compared 15, 30, and 60-minute infusions of the same dose on separate days [4]. The 60-minute infusion gave the least variable results, and the lowest normal gallbladder ejection fraction (the share of bile the gallbladder pushes out) was set at 38% [4]. The authors recommended that method as the standard [4].

The label also describes infusing sincalide over 50 minutes for gallbladder studies or 30 minutes for barium studies, as an alternative to a rapid injection, to lower the chance of stomach side effects [1].

The most frequent side effects, seen in 20% or more of people, are abdominal discomfort or pain and nausea [1]. A fast injection can also bring on brief vomiting, cramping, dizziness, or flushing, which is why slower infusions are an option [1]. Vasovagal reactions, a sudden drop in heart rate and blood pressure that can cause fainting, have also been reported [1].

Each vial contains sodium metabisulfite, and serious allergic reactions including anaphylactic shock have occurred during or soon after a dose, so people with a known sulfite or sincalide allergy should not receive it [1]. It is also not used when the bowel is blocked [1]. In people with small gallstones, the contraction can push a stone into a bile duct [1]. Because it acts on smooth muscle, it may carry a risk of preterm labour or miscarriage in pregnancy [1].
